dev.reply:
Yes
Having a committed five-family corpus before the red makes the work workable and fair. On parser and scrub changes, discovering missed edge cases (flags, volume specs, colon lists) in late fix rounds wastes significant developer time. Having explicit families, inputs, and expected outputs committed up front gives an unambiguous target to implement against during green, turning directly into clean parameterized unit test rows without gaming. The 20-minute counter-metric and 3-card trial guard against slice bloat.
CITE: each family with real inputs and the expected outputs
